steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing a diffusion-based terrain generation model that follows user sketches and produces climate-aware terrain detail.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Realistic, controllable terrain generation is hard
- Deep learning for terrain: GANs, then diffusion
- Our method: terrain diffusion network (TDN)
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Problem
  - real terrains shaped by climatic conditions: temperature variations, water/wind erosion, vegetation
  - automated generation must depict weather events and natural phenomena + follow user's structural guidance (controllability)
  - example-based and sketch-based methods compromise geologically precise fine-grained characteristics
  - need controllable synthesis with diverse, intricate, fine-grained features
- Deep learning
  - success in computer vision -> explored for high fidelity terrain generation
  - mostly GAN-based; trade-off between fidelity and divergence to user conditions
  - diffusion methods: wide variety of images from user prompts
  - potential: fine-grained diversity, climatic morphogenesis
  - challenge: stochastic nature vs user guidance
  - no existing controllable diffusion architecture for fine-grained, diversified terrain generation
- TDN
  - denoising Gaussian noise-perturbed terrain latent representations; follows user sketch guidance
  - sketches for rivers, ridges, basins, peaks (Fig. 1)
  - multi-level denoising scheme with terrain sketch encoder (structural consistency), replaces monolithic denoising
  - coarse-to-fine, multiple terrain synthesizers with direct user guidance: structural, intermediate, fine-grained
  - low-resolution inputs -> high-resolution outputs
  - different denoisor weights per stage; structural = overall components; fine-grained = climatic patterns, geomorphological erosion, tectonic events
  - lower-dimensional terrain and sketch latent spaces via pre-trained autoencoders for efficiency
- Contributions
  - deep learning approach with multiple geometric factors for controllable generation
  - multi-level denoising synthesizer, structural + fine-grained, climatic-aware
  - new dataset from NASA Topology Images; experiments show high-quality synthesis with flexible control

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In the real world terrains are affected by many climatic conditions, like temperature variations, erosion from water or wind, and vegetation. An automated terrain generation method has to depict such weather events and natural phenomena accurately, and it also has to follow the user's structural guidance closely for controllability so there are no unintended outcomes. But conventional controllable example-based and sketch-based methods often compromise on generating realistic terrains when it comes to geologically precise fine-grained characteristics. For the best fidelity we need more advanced controllable terrain synthesis techniques that can produce diverse and intricate features with fine granularity.

Deep learning techniques have been very successful for computer vision, so deep-learning methods have been explored for high fidelity terrain generation. Most of these studies use generative adversarial networks (GAN). But GANs still have a trade off between fidelity and divergence to user-provided conditions. Recently diffusion methods have shown promising results in generating a wide variety of images from user prompts. This means they could overcome the challenges of terrain generation: they give diversity at a fine-grained level and they could enable the generation of climatic morphogenesis. But there is a big challenge, because the diffusion model is stochastic by nature and this goes against the user's ability to guide terrain generation. As far as we know, no existing study has a controllable diffusion architecture for fine-grained and diversified terrain generation.

- TDN: denoise Gaussian noise-perturbed terrain latents, follow user sketch; sketches for rivers, ridges, basins, peaks (Fig. 1)
- multi-level denoising with terrain sketch encoder instead of monolithic denoising; coarse-to-fine; structural, intermediate, fine-grained synthesizers; low-res -> high-res
- separate denoisor weights per stage; structural vs fine-grained (climatic patterns, erosion, tectonic events)
- pre-trained autoencoders for lower-dimensional latents
- contributions: approach; multi-level synthesizer; NASA Topology Images dataset + experiments

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In the real world terrains are affected by many climatic conditions, like temperature variations, erosion from water or wind, and vegetation. An automated terrain generation method has to depict such weather events and natural phenomena accurately, and it also has to follow the user's structural guidance closely for controllability so there are no unintended outcomes. But conventional controllable example-based and sketch-based methods often compromise on generating realistic terrains when it comes to geologically precise fine-grained characteristics. For the best fidelity we need more advanced controllable terrain synthesis techniques that can produce diverse and intricate features with fine granularity.

Deep learning techniques have been very successful for computer vision, so deep-learning methods have been explored for high fidelity terrain generation. Most of these studies use generative adversarial networks (GAN). But GANs still have a trade off between fidelity and divergence to user-provided conditions. Recently diffusion methods have shown promising results in generating a wide variety of images from user prompts. This means they could overcome the challenges of terrain generation: they give diversity at a fine-grained level and they could enable the generation of climatic morphogenesis. But there is a big challenge, because the diffusion model is stochastic by nature and this goes against the user's ability to guide terrain generation. As far as we know, no existing study has a controllable diffusion architecture for fine-grained and diversified terrain generation.

So in this paper we propose a new deep learning method based on diffusion, called terrain diffusion network (TDN). It generates terrains by denoising Gaussian noise-perturbed terrain latent representations, and the terrains are realistic and visually appealing and follow the sketch guidance the user provides. With TDN users can explicitly define the structural-level terrain characteristics with their input sketches for rivers, ridges, basins, and peaks, as shown in Fig. 1. To take the user guidance into account properly, we design a multi-level denoising scheme with a terrain sketch encoder for structural consistency, which replaces the monolithic denoising in the conventional diffusion process. It uses a coarse-to-fine strategy with multiple terrain synthesizers that get direct user guidance, for structural, intermediate, and fine-grained geological patterns. This turns low-resolution inputs into high-resolution terrain outputs. Different denoisor weights are learnt for the different synthesis stages, so they can focus on different levels of terrain patterns. The structural synthesiser focuses more on the overall terrain components like rivers, ridges, basins, and peaks, and the fine-grained synthesiser adds more terrain details like climatic patterns including geomorphological erosion and tectonic events. To make TDN more efficient we also introduce terrain and sketch latent spaces with lower dimensions using pre-trained autoencoders.

The key contributions of this study are:

- • A new deep learning based approach that considers multiple geometric factors for controllable terrain generation.

- • A multi-level denoising synthesizer that formulates both structural and fine-grained terrain patterns, to produce realistic and climatic-aware terrain patterns.

- • A new dataset built from NASA Topology Images to evaluate how effective the proposed TDN is. Comprehensive experiments show that TDN can achieve high-quality realistic terrain synthesis with flexible user controls.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In the real world, terrains are subject to a variety of climatic conditions, such as temperature variations, erosion from water or wind, and the presence of vegetation. An automated terrain generation method must accurately depict such weather events and natural phenomena, while closely adhering to a user's structural guidance for controllability to avoid unintended outcomes. Yet, conventional controllable example-based and sketch-based methods [1,2] often compromise the generation of realistic terrains in terms of geologically precise fine-grained characteristics. Optimal fidelity requires more advanced controllable terrain synthesis techniques capable of producing diverse and intricate features with fine granularity.

Given the great success of deep learning techniques for computer vision [3,4,5,6], deep-learning methods have been explored for high fidelity terrain generation. Most of these studies are based on generative adversarial networks (GAN) [7,8]. However, GANs still suffer from a trade off between fidelity and divergence to user-provided conditions. Recently, diffusion methods [9] have shown promising results in generating a wide variety of images based on user prompts. This suggests significant potential to overcome the challenges of terrain generation: they foster diversity at a fine-grained level and offer the opportunity to generate climatic morphogenesis. Nonetheless, the inherent stochastic nature of diffusion models poses a significant challenge to the user's ability to guide the terrain generation process. To the best of our knowledge, no existing study offers a controllable diffusion architecture for fine-grained and diversified terrain generation.

Therefore, in this paper, we propose a novel deep learning method based on the diffusion approach, namely terrain diffusion network (TDN). It generates terrains by denoising Gaussian noise-perturbed terrain latent representations, producing realistic and visually appealing terrains that closely align with the user provided sketch guidance. TDN allows users to explicitly define structural-level terrain characteristics through input sketches for rivers, ridges, basins, and peaks, as shown in Fig. 1. To adequately account for user guidance, a multi-level denoising scheme with a terrain sketch encoder, aimed at structural consistency, is devised to replace the monolithic denoising of the conventional diffusion process. It employs a coarse-to-fine strategy, using multiple terrain synthesizers with direct user guidance to articulate structural, intermediate, and fine-grained geological patterns, transforming low-resolution inputs into high-resolution terrain outputs. Specifically, different denoisor weights are learnt for distinct synthesis stages, so that they can focus on different levels of terrain patterns. The structural synthesiser focuses on the overall terrain components, such as rivers, ridges, basins, and peaks, whilst the fine-grained synthesiser provides further terrain details such as climatic patterns including geomorphological erosion and tectonic events. To improve the efficiency of TDN, we further introduce terrain and sketch latent spaces with lower dimensions using pre-trained autoencoders.

In summary, the key contributions of this study are:

- • A novel deep learning based approach that takes multiple geometric factors into account for controllable terrain generation.

- • A multi-level denoising synthesizer that formulates both structural and fine-grained terrain patterns to produce realistic and climatic-aware terrain patterns.

- • A new dataset constructed from NASA Topology Images [10] to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed TDN. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that TDN achieves high-quality realistic terrain synthesis with flexible user controls.
